summary: For ages 5–7: build the idea that if you dig deep enough beneath the soil, grass and pavement (sometimes also through sand, clay or gravel), you reach rock, that the Earth is made mostly of rock and other materials, and that stones and pebbles are small pieces of the Earth's rock. Two complementary moves anchor the concept: DIG DOWN (from familiar ground through soil to bedrock) and ZOOM OUT (a held pebble is a tiny chip of the rocky planet). Keep to 'rock and other solid materials'; defer layers, heat and the core to a later 'Earth's Layers' topic for 7–9s. Confront the common beliefs that the Earth is dirt/soil all the way down, that it is hollow, and that stones are separate from the ground.
misconceptions: 'The Earth is made of soil/dirt' — soil is only a thin covering; solid rock lies beneath almost everywhere
'The Earth is hollow inside' — it is solid rock and other materials all the way down (interior detail comes later)
'Rocks and the ground are different things' — stones are broken-off pieces of the same Earth-rock
'Only mountains/cliffs are rock' — rock is under flat ground and under the sea too, just often hidden by soil or water
'The ground is just made of the stuff on top (grass, sand)' — those are thin surface layers over rock

activities.title: Dig down to the rock
steps: Start from a picture or cross-section of a familiar patch of ground — a garden, playground or beach.
Work down through the layers in order: grass, then a thin band of soil, then solid bedrock, then deeper rock.
Lift or reveal the soil layer to find the message underneath: 'just a thin skin — rock is underneath'.
Say aloud what is under the soil almost everywhere (rock), and how thin the soil is compared with the rock below.
Compare a real rock or stone in hand with the rock shown deep in the cross-section.
activities.insight: Soil is a thin covering compared with the rock beneath; dig deep enough (sometimes through sand, clay or gravel as well) and you reach solid rock almost everywhere, so the Earth is not dirt all the way down.

activities.title: Hands-on dig: how thin is the soil?
steps: Use a trowel or digging tool — a soil tray set up as a model of the ground, or an on-screen dig — to remove soil until you reach something hard.
Mark or measure how deep the soil goes before you reach the hard layer.
Describe out loud: the soil layer is thin, and in the real ground the rock keeps going far below it (in the tray or screen, the hard layer stands for that deep rock).
Handle real rock, stone and pebble samples and compare them with each other.
activities.insight: Removing the soil yourself in a model shows the idea that soil is a thin layer sitting on top of much more rock below — the tray or screen is a model of the real ground, so it represents the real depths rather than measuring them.

activities.title: Zoom out: a pebble is a piece of the Earth
steps: Hold a real pebble or stone and look at a picture of the whole Earth as a planet made mostly of rock.
Zoom out from the dug-down ground to the whole planet, seeing it as an enormous ball made mostly of rock.
Point to the pebble and state that it is a tiny piece of the Earth's rock.
Decide and explain whether a stone found on the ground is a piece of the Earth or a separate object.
activities.insight: Stones and pebbles are small pieces of the Earth's rock that have broken off and often been worn down — they are part of the Earth, not separate from it.

activities.title: Rock is everywhere, even where it's hidden
steps: Sort pictures or objects into 'made of rock' and 'not made of rock'.
Discuss where rock is hidden: under flat grass, under sand at the beach, and under the sea — not only in mountains and cliffs.
Answer: 'What is under the soil almost everywhere?' (rock, not water or empty space).
Talk about what is deep inside the Earth: rock and other materials, not empty space.
activities.insight: Rock is beneath flat ground and under the sea too, often hidden by soil, sand or water; the Earth is full of rock and other materials, not hollow.

checkQuestion: Imagine you could dig a deep, deep hole straight down — much deeper than a garden. What would you find most of the way down, and what is the Earth mostly made of underneath us?
checkAnswer: Just under the thin layer of soil at the top, it's mostly solid rock. The Earth is made of rock (and deeper still, very hot rock and metal). Soil is only a thin skin at the very top — the stones we find are pieces of that same rocky Earth.
